title: What does Git store when a file changes?
answer: Git writes only the objects whose bytes are new, and names unchanged content again by its id

checks.question: Starting again from commit one, a commit renames hello.txt to greeting.txt and changes nothing else. Which new objects does Git write, and why is no blob among them?
checks.answer: 2 objects, a tree and a commit. The name lives in the tree’s bytes, so the tree changes, and so does the commit that names it. The file’s bytes are unchanged, so its id is still ce01362 and the new tree names the stored blob.

checks.question: Starting again from commit one, a commit adds copy.txt containing exactly hello and a newline. How many new blobs does Git write?
checks.answer: None. Its bytes hash to ce01362, which is already stored, so the new tree lists both names against that one blob. The commit writes 2 objects, a tree and a commit.

checks.question: Two people on different machines each commit a file containing hello and a newline. Do their blobs have the same id? Do their commits?
checks.answer: The blobs do: both are ce01362, because a blob’s id depends only on its bytes. Commits match only if all their bytes match, including the tree, the parents, the author and committer lines with their timestamps, and the message, so in practice they differ.

steps.title: Git hashes 13 bytes to name this blob
steps.line: Predict: a second commit adds world.txt. Does Git store these bytes again?
steps.caption: A Git commit records a snapshot of the whole project, which sounds as if each commit copies all its files. Look at what Git stores for one file. hello.txt holds hello and a newline; Git puts a header with the type and length in front of those bytes and hashes the lot, and the 40-digit result names a blob. The file’s name is not among the hashed bytes, so any file holding exactly these bytes gets this same id, ce01362.
steps.picture: The content bytes "hello\n", one cell each with its hex value; The header bytes “blob 6” and a zero byte, in front of the content; An arrow labelled SHA-1 from the bytes to their id; The blob id ce013625030ba8dba906f756967f9e9ca394464a, its first seven digits highlighted; A brace under the first seven digits, ce01362: the name later pictures give the blob.

steps.title: A tree gives those bytes a name
steps.line: The name hello.txt is in the tree entry, not in the blob.
steps.caption: A tree associates the name hello.txt and its mode with the blob’s id. The same content object can therefore be named by different trees without copying it. Hashing the tree’s own bytes gives that collection of names and references an id too.

steps.title: A commit names a tree; a branch names a commit
steps.line: main → commit → tree → blob: each holds the next one’s id.
steps.caption: The branch main holds a commit’s id, and that commit names a tree. Following the references reaches the snapshot’s file names and contents. The commit describes the whole snapshot by naming objects that other commits can name too, without holding any file’s bytes itself.
